articles.title: Canada creates earthquake insurance backstop as Carney budget addresses decade-long gap
articles.summary: Budget 2026 proposes a Canadian Earthquake Insurance Facility that would give the P&C sector up to $50 billion in emergency funding after an extreme quake, closing a gap insurers have flagged since at least 2016. Legislation still has to pass, and IBC and IBAC will help design it. What this means for your business: if you operate in the Lower Mainland or on Vancouver Island, this should steady earthquake capacity over time, but now is the time to check your quake deductible, which is often a percentage of insured value, and your business interruption limits.

articles.title: Ukraine war risk insurance now 10 times more than Second World War Atlantic convoys
articles.summary: Lloyd's List reports Black Sea hull war premiums have reached about 20% as attacks intensify, a multi-decade high for any conflict zone. Middle East Gulf rates have eased to roughly 7% to 9% even with an estimated $2.5 billion in claims. What this means for your business: if you buy or sell goods moving through conflict regions, expect war-risk surcharges in freight quotes and confirm whether your cargo policy includes war and strikes cover or excludes those routes.

articles.title: Fridge cyber attack turns up heat on demand for cyber triggered physical damage cover
articles.summary: A November 2 attack on remotely managed refrigeration controllers pushed fridge and freezer temperatures up at supermarkets and food shops in six European countries, spoiling stock. CFC says the event shows a coverage gap, because cyber and property policies have long treated the digital trigger and the physical loss separately. What this means for your business: if you rely on connected equipment like refrigeration, HVAC or production controls, ask whether a hack that damages equipment or spoils inventory is covered by your cyber policy, your property policy, or neither.

articles.title: Department of Justice forms AI task force
articles.summary: The U.S. Justice Department has set up a Super Intelligence Task Force to coordinate its criminal and civil enforcement involving AI, set enforcement priorities and write guidance on prosecuting unlawful AI-related conduct. It absorbs the earlier AI Litigation Task Force. What this means for your business: if you sell into the U.S. or use AI in customer-facing decisions, fraud controls or marketing, expect closer regulatory scrutiny and check that your D&O and E&O policies would respond to a government investigation.

articles.title: Damages related to the use of AI: Italy allows direct lawsuits against the insurer. What's next?
articles.summary: Since September 30, a new Italian decree lets people harmed by the use of an AI system sue the at-fault party's liability insurer directly. It also lets courts order disclosure of how the AI works and presumes causation when AI Act obligations are breached. Clyde & Co expects more litigation, tighter wordings and AI questions on applications. What this means for your business: even in Canada, expect underwriters to ask more about which AI tools you use and how you supervise them, so keep an inventory of your AI tools ready before renewal.

articles.title: Russian hacker group claims to have posted B.C. school district information on dark web
articles.summary: CBC found what appears to be a database stolen from the Burnaby School District in a September breach posted on the leak site of the Qilin ransomware-as-a-service group. Screenshots show folders such as payroll, discipline and harassment investigations, and the files had been viewed thousands of times. What this means for your business: once data is stolen, it can sit online for weeks, so make sure your cyber policy covers notification, credit monitoring and privacy claims, not just restoring your systems.

articles.title: 'Risk is heightened everywhere': Tokio Marine Kiln's Pavlos Spyropoulos
articles.summary: Tokio Marine Kiln's APAC head says high-tech shipments tied to the AI boom are getting much more valuable and are being stolen more often, even as cargo rates keep falling. He also warns that rates are no longer adequate in some specialty lines, and political violence pricing has already started to firm. What this means for your business: if you ship electronics or other high-value components, check that your per-shipment and warehouse limits match today's values while soft-market pricing lasts.

articles.title: B.C. privacy watchdog launches investigation into Crime Stoppers data breach
articles.summary: B.C.'s Information and Privacy Commissioner is investigating whether B.C. Crime Stoppers took reasonable steps under PIPA to protect personal information, after a breach at its tip-platform vendor exposed more than 1.5 million tips nationwide. The federal privacy commissioner is also looking into it. What this means for your business: under B.C. law you remain responsible for personal data your vendors hold for you, so review vendor security terms and confirm your cyber policy covers breaches that happen at a third party.

articles.title: State bill allows consumers to hold AI chatbot providers liable
articles.summary: A proposed New Jersey bill would treat AI chatbots as products under the state's product liability law and allow $5,000 per violation plus action by the attorney general. Lawyers warn that statutory damages without proof of harm could produce large class-style claims. What this means for your business: if you put a chatbot in front of customers, review what it is allowed to say, read your vendor's indemnity, and check whether your liability policies carry AI exclusions.

articles.title: Is systemic cyber risk the next coverage frontier?
articles.summary: Cyber specialists at CFC and Hub look at July's rogue-AI-agent incident and conclude it was contained, not systemic, and that existing cyber policies respond to the loss types involved. Their bigger worry is concentration risk when many firms rely on the same AI vendors and cloud platforms. What this means for your business: list the AI and cloud vendors you depend on and confirm your cyber policy covers outages and breaches that start at a provider.

articles.title: AI agents are moving faster than human oversight – and insurers are taking notice
articles.summary: Lockton's AI risk lead says agent-to-agent transactions leave little room for meaningful human review, and some carriers are considering underwriting and pricing agentic AI deployments differently. Supplemental applications increasingly ask for an inventory of AI tools and who is responsible for each one. What this means for your business: if you provide professional or tech services using AI agents, tighten contract liability caps and indemnities first, then confirm your tech E&O limits match how far you have deployed AI.

articles.title: Why overseas shipping could leave your clients with cargo coverage gaps
articles.summary: Lockton Canada warns that exporters shifting sales from the U.S. to Europe and Asia face longer ocean transits, more terminal storage and bigger values sitting in one place than their cross-border cargo programs assumed. It also flags rising trailer and cargo theft, much of it never reported. What this means for your business: if your shipping routes have changed, review cargo limits, storage-in-transit cover and delay coverage before the next shipment, not at renewal.

articles.title: Credit insurers face rising insolvencies and tariff swings: Willis Re
articles.summary: Willis Re says trade credit loss ratios are returning to long-term norms as claims frequency rises. It points to forecasts of a fifth straight year of rising global insolvencies, oil near US$110, and U.S. tariff shifts. Construction, chemicals, retail and transport are flagged as most at risk. What this means for your business: if a few large customers make up much of your receivables, especially in those sectors or across the border, trade credit insurance or tighter credit terms are worth a look before the new year.

articles.title: Bill C-36: what Canada's proposed automated-decision rules would require
articles.summary: Ottawa's proposed Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act would require organizations to publicly describe automated decision systems and explain significant decisions to affected people, with penalties up to the greater of $25 million or 5% of global revenue. It is still awaiting second reading and is a privacy bill, not a full AI law. What this means for your business: if you use software to screen, price or approve customers or staff, start documenting how it works now, since regulatory and privacy claims usually follow new rules.

articles.title: OpenAI asks B.C. court to quash privacy commissioner investigation of Tumbler Ridge shooting
articles.summary: OpenAI has petitioned B.C. Supreme Court to quash the provincial privacy commissioner's investigation into how ChatGPT used personal information connected to the Tumbler Ridge shooter. It argues the probe exceeds the commissioner's authority and the production order is overbroad. The case will test how far B.C. privacy law reaches foreign AI services. What this means for your business: regulators are treating how AI tools use personal data as a privacy question, so know what customer data goes into the AI tools you use and what your vendor terms allow.

articles.title: Brokerages are now cyber targets too, Definity's MacDonald warns
articles.summary: A Definity executive told the IBAO convention that AI tools let attackers scan for weaknesses across thousands of small firms at once, so being small no longer keeps a business off the radar. He pointed to fast-growing privacy liability as a sign of how quickly per-client losses can add up. What this means for your business: assume you are a target, and make sure your cyber limits reflect how many customer records you actually hold.

articles.title: Cyber insurance's next big surprise?
articles.summary: Aviva and Intact executives at IBAOcon flagged cyber accumulation, where one attack on a shared service provider hits many companies at once, citing a European attack on grocery refrigeration systems. They also noted a wave of U.S. AI exclusions and urged basic prevention like dark-web scans. What this means for your business: ask whether your policy covers losses caused by an attack on a supplier or IT provider, not just on your own systems.

articles.title: Partial US tariff relief adds to valuation headaches for Canadian exporters and their insurers
articles.summary: A new U.S. proclamation dropped 50% duties on some Canadian goods such as plywood, paper and packaging from Oct. 30 while adding others like valves and carpets. Each swing changes replacement costs, revenue projections and customer finances. What this means for your business: recheck insured values, business-interruption figures, cargo limits and trade credit limits whenever tariffs move, and watch for U.S. buyers under strain.

articles.title: As rogue AI risks grow, insurers split on covering the damage
articles.summary: Some specialty insurers now sell affirmative AI cover through endorsements, tech E&O wording or standalone policies, while several large carriers are adding ISO exclusions for generative AI to general liability. The article also lists practical controls, from vendor contract reviews to limiting AI tool permissions. What this means for your business: coverage for AI mistakes now depends heavily on which insurer you're with, so it pays to compare wording, not just price.

articles.title: Canada commercial insurance rates fall for third straight year as market split deepens
articles.summary: Marsh's index shows Canadian commercial rates fell 6% in Q3 2026, led by an 8% drop in property, as strong insurer results and cheaper reinsurance expand capacity. Clean, Canada-only risks benefit most, while accounts with U.S. exposure, losses or catastrophe-exposed assets see tighter terms. What this means for your business: it's a buyer's market for well-documented risks, so good submission data can win real savings or broader cover at renewal.

articles.title: SME cyber insurance uptake stalls in Canada and everywhere except the US
articles.summary: CFC estimates only about 10-15% of small and mid-sized businesses in Canada carry standalone cyber cover, compared with 30-40% in the U.S., even though owners rank cyber as a top threat. The gap is blamed on how the market sells cover, not on owners being unaware. What this means for your business: if you rely on a small cyber add-on to your package policy, check whether its limits would cover a real ransomware recovery.

articles.title: Small businesses insure the building and overlook shutdown and cyber risk, Wawanesa VP says
articles.summary: A Wawanesa executive says many small businesses insure their premises but leave out business interruption and cyber, often believing they are too small to be targeted. Walking through a worst-case shutdown tends to reveal the gap. What this means for your business: estimate how long you could survive closed after a fire, flood or hack, and make sure income and cyber cover match that number.

articles.title: EU AI Act: AI Omnibus adopted
articles.summary: The EU's AI Omnibus pushes back high-risk AI obligations to December 2027 for standalone systems and August 2028 for AI built into regulated products, but transparency and general-purpose AI rules still apply. Canadian firms selling AI-enabled products or services into Europe remain in scope. What this means for your business: the extra time is a window to build compliance records, and contracts with EU customers may still demand AI Act warranties today.

articles.title: AI exclusions struggle to gain traction
articles.summary: Brokers and carriers including EPIC, Willis, Zurich and Coalition say broad AI exclusions are meeting resistance because AI is now part of everyday operations, and most insurers prefer to handle it through underwriting. Some affirmative AI covers can still act as hidden exclusions. What this means for your business: read any AI language on your renewal closely, because a broker can often negotiate it away or find a market that doesn't use it.

articles.title: Does AI need its own insurance market? Brokers are already finding out
articles.summary: Standalone AI liability products from Armilla, Munich Re's aiSure and others now cover model errors, inaccurate outputs and AI agent actions, sometimes paired with cyber and tech E&O. Half of brokers polled expect AI insurance to become a major line of its own. What this means for your business: if you build or resell AI tools, a tech E&O policy alone may not respond to a model failure, so ask about dedicated AI performance cover.

articles.title: CIRA survey: Canadian organizations spend more on cybersecurity, but fewer believe it's enough
articles.summary: CIRA's 2026 survey of 503 Canadian decision-makers found most raised cybersecurity budgets, yet only 67% think spending keeps pace with threats, down from 74% a year earlier. The share of organizations with very small IT budgets also doubled. What this means for your business: when the budget can't cover every control, insurance and an incident response plan become the backstop, and insurers reward the basics like MFA and backups.

articles.title: Silent or affirmative: the AI coverage debate reshaping Canadian cyber placements
articles.summary: Canadian clients are pushing for cyber wording that names AI and deepfakes, after cases like a US$25.6 million deepfake video-call fraud. Hub's cyber lead explains why some brokers prefer explicit wording and others worry it narrows cover. What this means for your business: confirm your policy covers social-engineering fraud by deepfake voice or video, and train staff to verify payment requests by a second channel.

articles.title: ISO's generative AI exclusion is already on thousands of CGL policies
articles.summary: ISO's generative AI exclusions for general liability took effect in January and have been adopted by several major U.S. carriers, with Berkley also using an absolute AI exclusion on D&O and E&O. No standard replacement product yet fills the gap. What this means for your business: map where you use AI before renewal, since exclusions found early are far easier to negotiate than ones found at claim time.
